summary.text: Newton's three laws of motion describe how forces change the movement of bodies, and he first stated them in 1687.
A body stays at rest or moves steadily in a straight line unless a force acts, and the net force equals its mass times its acceleration.
When two bodies exert forces on each other, those forces are equal in size and opposite in direction.

facts.label: First law
facts.value: Motion continues unchanged unless a force acts

facts.label: Second law
facts.value: Net force equals mass times acceleration

facts.label: Third law
facts.value: Mutual forces are equal and opposite

facts.label: Force is a vector
facts.value: It has both size and direction

items.prompt: You sit in a windowless train gliding smoothly at constant speed. Can an experiment show whether you or the platform is really moving?

options.label: No, since no inertial observer is privileged over another
Yes, because the train carries your motion with it
Yes, but only if the train speeds up a lot
No, but only because the train is so large

items.explain: There is no absolute standard of rest, and no experiment can say which inertial observer is really moving.

items.prompt: A girl pushes a wall and the wall pushes back equally hard, yet nothing cancels out. Why?

options.label: The wall's push is only felt, not real
The two forces act on different bodies
The forces differ in size by a small amount
Only the stronger force of the two counts

items.explain: The action and reaction apply to different bodies, so they do not cancel on a single body.

items.prompt: The same push is given to an empty shopping cart and a full one. Why does the empty cart speed up more?

options.label: Heavier carts feel less of the push
Empty carts have less friction in every case
The same net force gives less acceleration to more mass
Acceleration depends only on the push's direction

items.explain: Net force equals mass times acceleration, so with the same force a larger mass gets a smaller acceleration.

items.prompt: A puck slides on frictionless ice in a straight line at steady speed. What is the net force on it?

options.label: A small forward force that keeps it going
A force equal to its weight
A force that grows as time passes
Zero

items.explain: Motion at constant speed in a straight line continues without a force, so the net force is zero and the body does not accelerate.

items.prompt: When can the Earth reasonably be treated as a single point?

options.label: When working out how a ball bounces on its surface
When working out its orbit around the Sun
When working out how a car drives on a road
When working out how deep a well must be

items.explain: Earth can be pointlike for its orbit around the Sun but not for activities on its surface.

items.prompt: A friend says a push is fully described by how hard it is. What is missing from that description?

options.label: Which way it points, since force is a vector
How long the push has existed in the world
Which person happened to make the push
Whether the push came from a rope or a hand

items.explain: Force is a vector quantity, and a vector has both magnitude and direction.
